b65588bcfd.q: What does a business owe to the community that built it?
b65588bcfd.a: No business becomes successful on its own. Somebody had to believe in you, hire you, buy from you, refer you, work for you, or give you another chance when you made a mistake. A community helped make your success possible. When a company becomes successful, that success creates an opportunity for responsibility—not from guilt, but from stewardship of what has been placed in your hands.
b65588bcfd.e: If Your Company Vanished Tomorrow Would Anyone Care
b65588bcfd.rq: If generosity isn't part of who you are when you have a little, there's a pretty good chance it won't suddenly become part of who you are when you have a lot.

57550aaa8a.q: Does giving back to the community always require money?
57550aaa8a.a: Absolutely not. Money is a resource, but think in terms of time, people, knowledge, equipment, vehicles, relationships, space, social media platforms, audience, and expertise. Sometimes the greatest contribution isn't money—it's the ability to mobilize people. A contractor can use team skills to repair a home, a marketing company can help a nonprofit improve its message, or a company can allow team members to volunteer together.

34bd4805cf.q: How can businesses distinguish between genuine community involvement and using it as a marketing tool?
34bd4805cf.a: It's about intention. Are you helping because you care, or because you want somebody to know that you helped? There's a difference. If the story focuses on the community need and how to help rather than on how amazing your company is, you've changed the focus. The community can't become a prop for your advertising campaign. You help someone simply because helping them matters—if content comes from that, that's fine, but that's not the reason you showed up.

418c1461f4.q: Why should businesses focus on a few community causes rather than trying to support everything?
418c1461f4.a: There are so many needs—homelessness, addiction, food insecurity, veterans, children, education, recovery, families with illness, nonprofits. Companies can't do everything and shouldn't try. Find the things that connect with the heart of your organization and where your resources can actually make a difference. Consistency is key—it's better to be deeply committed to two or three things year after year than to jump from cause to cause because something becomes popular for the month. Consistency builds trust and real relationships.

91efea3511.q: What should happen if your company disappeared tomorrow—would the community miss your impact?
91efea3511.a: This is a challenging question to reflect on. Would an organization say your company always showed up for them? Would families miss something you helped provide? Would young people lose an opportunity? Would a nonprofit lose volunteers or a cause lose supporters? Would people say your company made the community better because you were here? That's the measure of whether you've truly made an impact beyond just being a business.
